EXPERIMENTAL TEACHING MODEL

THE VIRTUAL PHYSIOLOGY LABORATORY

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing

A ramp test on a cycle ergometer. Work rises every second until a link in the O2 chain gives out: the lungs, gas exchange, the heart, the blood, or the muscles. Find what stopped each patient.

StaticsPulmonary function testsExercise testing

Experimental teaching model · Subject: 40-year-old man, 80 kg, 25 W/min ramp. Protocol: 2 min rest, 2 min unloaded pedaling, the ramp, then recovery. Each patient’s ramp rate is chosen so the ramp lasts about 8 to 12 minutes, as in a clinical lab. Not for patient care.

THINK THROUGH THE RESULTS

CPET report

Flagged: VO2max below 85% of predicted; peak heart rate at or below 85%; other peak values below 80%; respiratory reserve below 30%; peak R below 1.10; V̇E/V̇CO2 at AT above 34; a fall in SpO2 of 4 points or more. Flagged values are bold red and the row is marked with an asterisk; times on the charts are minutes from the start of the test

INTERPRETATIONDecide what limited this patient, then show the stepwise interpretation

    Cutoffs from the course reading (Milani 2006): VO2max below 85% of predicted is reduced; an anaerobic threshold below 40% of predicted VO2max is low; respiratory reserve (also called breathing reserve: 1 − peak V̇E/MVV) below 30% is ventilatory impairment (20–30% borderline); peak heart rate at or below 85% of predicted means the heart did not reach its maximum; peak R below 1.10 suggests a submaximal effort. Heart rate reserve here is predicted maximum minus peak heart rate, as in exercise testing (not the resting-based reserve used to prescribe exercise). VE/VCO2 above 34 is inefficient ventilation (ATS/ACCP 2003). Beyond the lecture: O2 pulse, heart rate reserve, MVV, the numeric cutoffs, and the disease patterns are clinical extensions of the lecture’s ideas (linear V̇O2, anaerobic threshold, R, ventilatory equivalents, cardiac limitation).

    HOW THE TEST WORKS

    Following O2 from air to muscle

    The patient breathes through a mouthpiece while pedaling against a resistance that rises steadily. Each breath is analyzed for flow, O2, and CO2, giving V̇O2, V̇CO2, and V̇E; ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry run throughout. Every link in the chain from lungs to circulation to muscle must keep up, and the first one that cannot stops the test.

    V̇O2 = HR × SV × (CaO2 − CvO2)

    In health the heart is the ceiling: heart rate reaches its predicted maximum and breathing reserve is left over. Cardiac output rises from about 6 to 20–25 L/min, and mixed venous saturation falls from about 75% toward 40–50% as muscles extract more O2. In health, then, we are cardiac limited, with plenty of respiratory reserve. The highest V̇O2 reached is the VO2max (strictly, peak V̇O2 unless V̇O2 plateaus). Even healthy lungs show a wider A-a gradient at peak exercise. Highly trained athletes can desaturate a few points. At their very high cardiac outputs, red cells pass through the lung capillaries too fast to load fully, ventilation-perfusion matching worsens, and ventilation may not rise enough to make up for it (Dempsey & Wagner 1999). O2 pulse is the O2 taken up per heartbeat (V̇O2/HR). By Fick it equals stroke volume times the a-v O2 difference, so it is low when stroke volume cannot rise or the blood carries less O2.

    V̇E = 0.863 · V̇CO2 / [PaCO2 · (1 − VD/VT)]

    This is the alveolar ventilation equation rearranged; 0.863 converts the units (V̇CO2 in mL/min, PaCO2 in mmHg, V̇E in L/min).

    Ventilation follows CO2 output, first by deeper breaths, then faster ones. The respiratory exchange ratio, RER (R, V̇CO2/V̇O2), climbs gradually as the muscles burn more carbohydrate. Above the anaerobic threshold, bicarbonate buffers lactic acid and releases extra CO2, so V̇CO2 and V̇E rise faster than V̇O2 and RER climbs above 1. Later, buffering can no longer keep up. Ventilation then rises even faster and PaCO2 falls; that point is the respiratory compensation point (RCP). Dead space volume grows with exercise (the airways stretch, and V/Q mismatch adds some alveolar dead space), but tidal volume grows more, so the dead space fraction VD/VT falls. A high dead space fraction (heart failure, pulmonary vascular disease, lung disease) raises V̇E/V̇CO2: more ventilation is wasted for each liter of CO2 removed. The lungs only limit exercise when V̇E approaches the maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV). MVV can be measured directly; here it is estimated as FEV1 × 40, an estimate that works best in obstruction and is rougher in restrictive disease. Healthy untrained people finish with 30–50% of their MVV unused (the respiratory reserve); only highly trained athletes come close to it.

    Model details. V̇O2 demand is 3.5 mL/kg/min at rest, plus 150 mL/min for unloaded pedaling, plus 10.3 mL/min per watt, with 45 s on-kinetics. The circulatory limit is HRmax × SVmax (135 mL, so peak cardiac output about 24 L/min) × CaO2 × maximal extraction (60%, mixed venous saturation about 40%, the lecture’s values); heart rate rises linearly with V̇O2. Once work demands more than that ceiling, the extra is paid for anaerobically, and the test ends when that reserve runs out; a breathless patient stops sooner, before much lactate builds up, and a patient who gives less than full effort stops before reaching either ceiling. A faster ramp piles up work faster, so peak work ends further above what peak V̇O2 predicts. The anaerobic threshold sits about 55% of the way from rest to the circulatory limit, rising toward 75% with endurance training. RER rises from 0.83 at rest to about 0.97 at AT; above AT, V̇CO2 gains another 0.45 mL per mL of extra V̇O2; past the respiratory compensation point PaCO2 falls by up to 4 mmHg. VD/VT falls from its resting value (0.33 in health, higher in lung and heart disease) toward its peak value. In heart failure a stronger drive to breathe also lowers PaCO2; the model's dead space setting stands in for every cause of a high V̇E/V̇CO2. Tidal volume plateaus at 60% of VC, and breathing rate makes up the rest. Predicted V̇O2max = weight × (50.72 − 0.372 × age) for men (Hansen, Sue & Wasserman 1984); predicted HRmax = 220 − age; predicted MVV uses the PFT page's healthy FEV1. Not modeled: blood pressure, ECG, lactate, dynamic hyperinflation, and the slow component of V̇O2.
